tier_reason: The numbers are the project's own benchstat output in the README 'Benchmark' section. The benchmark code is public (benchmark/Makefile, benchmark/main_test.go, main_fbs.go, main_km.go, main_native_fbs.go, main_native_km.go, main_wasi_bench_test.go) and the hardware is stated (Apple M1), but no Go or TinyGo toolchain version is given for the run. That makes it first-party with partial methodology, which is C, not B: no peer review and no independent suite (alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks does not include Karmem).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: 'almost 10 times faster than Google Flatbuffers'. benchstat, FlatBuffers (old) vs Karmem (new), Apple M1. Native: EncodeObjectAPI 2.54ms -> 0.51ms (-79.85%, ~5x), DecodeObjectAPI 3.57ms -> 0.20ms (-94.30%, ~18x), DecodeSumVec3 1.44ms -> 0.16ms (-88.86%, ~9x). WASM on wazero: EncodeObjectAPI 17.2ms -> 4.0ms (-76.51%, ~4.3x), DecodeObjectAPI 50.7ms -> 1.9ms (-96.18%, ~27x), DecodeSumVec3 5.74ms -> 0.75ms (-86.87%, ~7.7x). The x-ratios are derived from page data. Allocations are zero only natively: 0 vs 1.00k allocs/op for encode and 0 vs 110k for decode. Under WASM allocs/op are about equal (4 vs 4 encode, 4 vs 5 decode).
corrections.workload: Go testing benchmarks in benchmark/ (main_test.go, main_fbs.go, main_km.go). They encode and decode, through the object API, a Monsters root of 1000 monsters; each monster has a 100-element Vec3 path, a 100-byte inventory, weapons, hitbox and status arrays. DecodeSumVec3 sums the path vectors with zero-copy readers. The FlatBuffers side uses the Go object API (Pack / UnPackTo) with a 'similar', not identical, schema. Runs cover native Go and a TinyGo-compiled WASI module inside wazero, on an Apple M1.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go and TinyGo versions for the README run are unstated. benchmark/go.mod declares go 1.18 and FlatBuffers Go v2.0.6; CI (.builds/ubuntu.yml) uses go1.18.4 on linux/amd64, but that is not the M1 run. Native: go test -tags fbs|km -bench=. -benchmem -benchtime=5s -count 5. WASM: tinygo build -target wasi -gc conservative --no-debug -opt 2 -scheduler none, run under wazero. Results compared with benchstat.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark only; no Go/TinyGo toolchain version is stated for the M1 run, which caps it below A. The FlatBuffers baseline goes through the Go object API (Pack/UnPackTo, very allocation-heavy: 110k allocs/op on decode) rather than FlatBuffers' idiomatic zero-copy accessors, except in DecodeSumVec3, where the gap is still ~9x natively. The schemas are 'similar', not identical: Karmem uses inline fixed arrays ([5]float64, [4]Weapon) where FlatBuffers uses vectors. Hacker News commenters (item 32302120) questioned the methodology and the '10x' claim, and the author did not answer those points in the thread. The README warns that the API is not stable. No commits since 2023-03-03 (>3 years), so abandoned.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly. Tier lowered from B to C because this is the project's own benchmark without toolchain versions, not an independent suite. The 'zero allocations' part of the claim holds only for native Go, not WASM. Metadata (BSD-3-Clause, 683 stars, last commit 2023-03-03, not archived, not a fork) is all confirmed.

tier_reason: The results table sits in glycerine/go_serialization_benchmarks, a personal fork (8 stars) where ZebraPack's author added ZebraPack and ran the numbers himself (commits 2016-2017 by Jason E. Aten). The upstream alecthomas suite never included ZebraPack, so these are first-party numbers, not an independent suite. The code is public (serialization_benchmarks_test.go) and Go 1.8beta2 is stated, but the CPU is only '3.1 GHz Intel Core i7' with no model, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Fork README, sorted by write speed: ZebraPackMarshal 120 ns/op, 0 B/op, is the fastest marshal in the table. Against the others: GogoprotobufMarshal 152 ns/op (~1.27x), FlatBufferMarshal 379 ns/op (~3.2x), CapNProtoMarshal (glycerine/go-capnproto v1) 498 ns/op (~4.2x), GoprotobufMarshal (golang/protobuf) 500 ns/op (~4.2x), ProtobufMarshal (DeDiS/protobuf, reflection-based, not Google's) 936 ns/op (~7.8x). Ratios derived from page data. Read side: ZebraPackUnmarshal 236 ns/op ties FlatBuffers (236) and is slower than Gencode (196), CapNProto v1 (210) and GreenPack (224). It is ~3.0x faster than Goprotobuf (701, derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: Protocol Buffers (golang/protobuf, gogo/protobuf, DeDiS/protobuf), Cap'n Proto (glycerine/go-capnproto v1, zombiezen capnproto2), FlatBuffers
corrections.workload: The glycerine fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks (serialization_benchmarks_test.go): go test -bench Marshal/Unmarshal of a 6-field struct A (Name, BirthDay, Phone, Siblings, Spouse, Money), picked at random from 1000 pre-generated values, across ~19 Go serializers. The ZebraPack marshal appends into a pre-allocated 512-byte buffer that is reused on every call.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.8beta2 per the README header. That header predates the Aug-2017 re-run that added GreenPack and produced the current table, so it may be stale. Command: go test -bench='.*'; no other flags stated.
corrections.hardware: 3.1 GHz Intel Core i7 (MacBook Pro 13"); exact CPU model unstated
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers: ZebraPack's author ran them in his own fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks, and the upstream suite (1.6k stars) never added ZebraPack. The table is from 2017, and its 'Go 1.8beta2' header may be stale. The author's own README says the read ranking 'varies occasionally run-by-run'. The marshal lead is small against gogoprotobuf (~1.27x). ZebraPack marshals into a reused pre-allocated buffer while goprotobuf and DeDiS allocate per call. The 'Protobuf' row is DeDiS reflection-based protobuf, and 'CapNProto' is the author's own go-capnproto v1. The repo points to GreenPack (same author) as 'a more recent alternative'. No commits since 2018-11-07 (>3 years), so abandoned.

notes: Every number in the record appears on the page in ZebraPack's rows. Tier lowered from B to C because the shootout run was the author's own, not an independent suite. Two row names were misattributed: 'ProtobufMarshal' is DeDiS/protobuf, not Google protobuf, and the gogoprotobuf margin (~1.27x) was omitted. Metadata (MIT, 171 stars, last commit 2018-11-07, not archived, not a fork) is confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party size table in the README, measured against Python's msgpack. The benchmark inputs are public (benchmark/*.json), but there is no benchmark script, and no toolchain or hardware is given, so it is C. The tier is unchanged. The verdict is downgrade only because the claim overstated the win count: it is 6 of 10 cases, not 7.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Smaller than MessagePack on 6 of 10 test cases: log entries 10.9 KB vs 15.1 KB (~28% smaller), flat records 2.1 KB vs 4.0 KB, hex strings 1.9 KB vs 3.4 KB, sparse nulls 903 B vs 1.9 KB (~52% smaller), repeated strings 557 B vs 1.2 KB (~54% smaller), deep nesting 18 B vs 25 B. Larger than MessagePack on 4 of 10: float array 4.8 KB vs 4.4 KB, int array 3.1 KB vs 2.6 KB, bool array 940 B vs 503 B, tiny objects 11 B vs 10 B. Percentages derived from page data.
corrections.caveats: A first-party, size-only benchmark with no benchmark script in the repo; benchmark/ holds only the 10 input JSON files. The results are honestly mixed: fernBuffer is larger than MessagePack on 4 of 10 cases, and the README notes dense int arrays at ~2.19x MsgPack size. The README calls it 'a prototype / proof of concept'. The core is actually C++ (fernbuffer.cpp and src/*.hpp, depending on nlohmann/json) behind a C API. Tiny, single-author, very new: 3 commits, all on 2026-06-07, 6 stars. The verifier recomputed the MsgPack column from the benchmark JSON files and matched all 10 values; the fernBuffer sizes were not reproduced (no build).

notes: The README table matches the record's numbers, but the record said 7/10 wins; the table shows 6/10. The language field says C, but the repo is a C++ implementation with a C header (not a correctable field here). The MsgPack sizes were independently reproduced exactly from the repo's benchmark inputs. Metadata (MIT, 6 stars, last commit 2026-06-07, active) is confirmed.
